themes.title: Bank and airline outages, and a cyber-attack claim the banks have not backed
themes.summary: Accounts on the feed circulated reports of Monday outages at major U.S. banks and a separate system outage at United Airlines. Those disruptions were real: a technical problem at JPMorgan Chase delayed online banking and some transactions involving Chase at other banks, and service was restored by evening; United said a system outage delayed departures for a few hours. Several widely shared posts, including one from @GenFlynn, suggested the outages were “probably a cyber attack.” Chase has said a software bug caused its outage and that it was not a cyberattack. No major outlet has reported that the bank and airline incidents were connected or were a cyberattack.
themes.whyItMatters: A real outage can still be wrapped in a claim that goes further than the evidence. Readers who bank or fly need the confirmed disruption, not the unverified explanation.

flags.label: Confirmed
flags.note: The bank and United outages were real and are documented in official and wire reporting.

flags.label: Disputed
flags.note: The cyber-attack claim is not supported. Chase attributed its outage to a software bug.

themes.title: Elon Musk says the FAA turned down free Starlink terminals
themes.summary: @elonmusk wrote that “Free Starlinks for FAA were offered to Sec Duffy, but he said they were not needed. As it turns out, they were.” The offer and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s reply are Musk’s own account. Neither Duffy nor the Department of Transportation has confirmed that exchange in reporting we checked. Coverage of the Nov. 13 FAA ground stop has described a router installation that flooded an older network with data; it is not clear Starlink would have prevented that problem.
themes.whyItMatters: This was one of the most-shared posts in the feed. It is presented here as Musk’s claim, not as a confirmed decision by the FAA.

flags.label: Unverified
flags.note: The offer and Duffy’s answer have not been independently confirmed by Duffy or DOT.

themes.title: A “dirty bomb” threat and a change of presidential aircraft were linked in the feed
themes.summary: @JesseBWatters asked whether a “dirty bomb” threat in Washington explained airline problems, bank outages and a diversion of Air Force One, writing that the government was “telling us EVERYTHING is fine.” Two of those items have some basis in reporting, but not as one event. CNN, cited by other outlets, reported that U.S. intelligence indicates Iran is developing plans that could include a dirty bomb in Washington; the White House has said there are no credible threats to the homeland right now. Separately, the Washington Post reported that President Trump flew to Asia on a less secure plane, and ABC reported that intelligence officials had judged a threat to him not credible before that switch. No outlet we checked has tied the plane change, or Monday’s bank and airline outages, to a dirty-bomb plot.
themes.whyItMatters: Packaging several disruptions as one plot is how a feed can outrun the reporting. The pieces are being checked as separate stories.

flags.label: Partly confirmed
flags.note: Reporting exists on an Iran dirty-bomb concern and, separately, on a change of presidential aircraft.

flags.label: Disputed
flags.note: No outlet we checked has connected the plane change or Monday’s outages to a dirty-bomb threat.

source.title: Washington Post on the aircraft change

themes.title: Freeman Johnson, 106, and Pizza Hut co-founder Dan Carney, 95
themes.summary: Two death notices spread widely. @StevenErtelt and @DailyLoud reported that Freeman Johnson, described as the oldest known Pearl Harbor survivor, had died at 106. AP, USA Today and the Guardian report that Johnson died at his home in Centerville, Massachusetts. He was a 21-year-old sailor aboard the USS St. Louis on Dec. 7, 1941. @DailyLoud also reported that Pizza Hut co-founder Dan Carney had died at 95. That is confirmed: he died Nov. 13 in Wichita, Kansas. He and his brother Frank opened the first Pizza Hut there in 1958 with $600 borrowed from their mother.
themes.whyItMatters: These were among the most-engaged news posts in the feed, and both check out against independent obituaries.

flags.label: Confirmed
flags.note: Both deaths are confirmed by wire and local reporting.

themes.title: James O’Keefe’s first court appearance in Minneapolis
themes.summary: @JamesOKeefeIII said sheriff’s deputies had to escort him past a “mob” outside a Minneapolis courthouse and later wrote that there was “no police presence outside.” The court date is confirmed: O’Keefe and Cam Higby made their first appearance Monday on felony identity-theft and unlawful-voting charges tied to Aug. 11 primary videos in which they falsely told election judges they were registered voters. They were released without bail, did not enter pleas, and are due back Jan. 13. MPR News described groups of supporters and opponents outside, including “a small handful of protesters,” and did not report assaults. The “mob” and assault claims have not been independently confirmed.
themes.whyItMatters: The charges and the appearance are on the record. The street scene he described is his account, and local reporting describes a smaller protest than “mob” suggests.

flags.label: Confirmed
flags.note: The Monday court appearance and the charges are confirmed by MPR News and Courthouse News.

flags.label: Unverified
flags.note: The “mob” and assault claims were not corroborated in local reporting we checked.

themes.title: Andy Lee on Carney’s China trip, a 2023 Barton payment, and Telesat’s debt
themes.summary: @RealAndyLeeShow posted several Canada items. A video clip had Prime Minister Mark Carney, before meeting Xi Jinping, saying that if Canada’s auto plants cannot be fully used in a North American market because of U.S. trade actions, Canada would look at other options, including Chinese investment, with a condition of real Canadian manufacturing — a comment confirmed by AP and the Guardian. She later quoted Carney after the Shenzhen meeting; the meeting’s results are confirmed: China expanded tariff relief to about C$400 million of Canadian exports, and Canada extended exemptions on 32 Chinese steel and aluminum items. A separate post asked about a $148,059 payment to “Dominic Stephen Barton” listed in the 2023 Public Accounts under Global Affairs Canada’s “Other Services.” The listing is on the record; what the payment was for has not been publicly explained. Barton, now chair of the Invest in Canada Hub, was scheduled to appear by video Tuesday at the Commons trade committee. Another post quoted older discussion of Telesat debt coming due; on Nov. 16 Telesat said it had reached a standstill with lenders to its GEO unit until Jan. 18, 2027.
themes.whyItMatters: These posts are among the few Canada-policy threads in a feed that is otherwise heavily U.S.-focused, and they overlap with reporting we published on the Carney–Xi meeting.

flags.label: Confirmed
flags.note: Carney’s auto-investment comments and the Shenzhen meeting results are confirmed by official and wire reporting.

flags.label: Unverified
flags.note: The 2023 Barton payment appears in the Public Accounts; its purpose has not been publicly explained.

themes.title: Beyoncé becomes the first artist with 100 Grammy nominations
themes.summary: @DailyLoud wrote that Beyoncé “has officially made GRAMMY HISTORY, becoming the first artist ever to reach 100 career Grammy nominations.” That is confirmed by Billboard and Grammy.com. Her 100th nomination is Best R&B Solo Performance for “Morning Dew (Donk)” at the 2027 Grammys. Grammy talk also showed up on X’s Canada trending list this morning, alongside The Game Awards.
themes.whyItMatters: It is a clean, checkable milestone, and it is one of the few entertainment stories that cut through a news-heavy feed.

flags.label: Confirmed
flags.note: Billboard and Grammy.com both report the 100-nomination mark.

themes.title: Older stories recirculated as if they had just happened
themes.summary: Three high-engagement posts in the 24-hour window were about events from mid-October or earlier this month. @libsoftiktok wrote that Pastor Steve Maile, “arrested in the UK after publicly criticizing Islam, just had his charges DROPPED.” Police did close the case, but he was never charged: the case was closed with “no further action” on Oct. 27 because the evidence did not meet the bar for charges. A second @libsoftiktok post said Dara O’Connor “was just sentenced to 24 months” for trying to burn down a possible ICE warehouse in Missouri. The sentence is real — 24 months in federal prison and two years of supervised release after a guilty plea to having two unregistered destructive devices — but it was handed down on Oct. 28. @TrumpDailyPosts wrote that “President Trump was cleared of any criminal activities in relation to Epstein” after a 15-month congressional investigation, and that “lamestream media just glossed over” it. The Republican-majority House Oversight report, released Nov. 10, did say it found no documents implicating Trump in criminal activity and that witnesses told the committee that, to their knowledge, he was not involved. Most of the report is about failures in the federal investigations. Whether news outlets “glossed over” it is the poster’s opinion.
themes.whyItMatters: A “BREAKING” label or the word “just” can make a weeks-old case look like today’s news. The underlying records are real; the timing and, in the Maile post, the wording are not.

flags.label: Older story
flags.note: The Maile case was closed Oct. 27, the O’Connor sentence was Oct. 28, and the Oversight report was released Nov. 10.

flags.label: Disputed
flags.note: Maile was investigated for months but was never charged; “charges dropped” overstates the record.
